note.question: How does queue-length information prior to traveling affect customers’ decision to travel?
note.overview: The model considers a service system in which customers must travel to the queue to be served. In our base model, customers observe the queue length and then decide whether to travel. We also consider alternative information models and investigate how the availability of queue-length information affects customer-equilibrium strategies, throughput, and social welfare.

source.quote: Managerial implications: Our results imply that when system congestion is high, the provider can increase throughput by disclosing the queue-length information, whereas at low congestion, the provider benefits from concealing the information.
Problem definition: We consider a service system in which customers must travel to the queue to be served.
In other models, the locations for the service facilities are decision variables (Berman and Krass 2015 and section 11.2.3 in Hassin 2016).

From the provider’s point of view, disclosing information is favorable when the system’s potential congestion is high or when the population that aims to use the service is spread over a larger area, implying higher expected travel time.
Because customers travel simultaneously, we model the traveling queue as a system of an inﬁnite number of servers.
